Logging to local or network paths detected
 Mandatory 3
FilePosition
src\eShopLegacyMVC\log4Net.xml

Explanation

Logging to local or network paths detected.

If you are targeting Managed Instance on Azure App Service, prefer Application Insights/App Service logging. If filesystem logs are required, write to a mounted Azure Files share configured via storage mounts and Key Vault secrets.

Logging APIs that write to disk might not work on Azure App Service or Container.

Use logging that stores logs in locations outside of the host unless its specifically required by your app. You can also use logging capabilities embedded in Azure, such as Azure App Service logging or Application Insights.

For migrating to AKS, use LogMonitor tool that can capture logs written to files, the console, or write logs and redirect them to Azure.

Explanation

Your application has local or network IO operations.

If you are targeting Managed Instance on Azure App Service, move persistent I/O to storage mounts (Azure Files/UNC). Keep local writes to temp only; connect to external dependencies via private endpoints/VNet to reduce latency.

IO operations outside of the application folder might not be available on Azure App Service. Review and ensure IO APIs are attempting to access paths that will be available when your app is running on App Service sandbox. If you choose the containerized hosting option, your scenario still might be broken or have scalability issues.

Possible solutions:
1. Files that the application needs can be deployed with the application or put in Azure Storage. You can use Azure Storage File Shares as a drop-in replacement for on-premises file share.
2. Other services that the application depends on might need to be migrated to Azure, this way you will get the benefit of lower latency in the cloud.
3. If your application needs to depend on services that run on-premise, you can connect your Azure and local networks with ExpressRoute, Hybrid Connections, or VPN solutions.

Local OS environment access detected
 Potential 1
FilePosition
src\eShopLegacyMVC\Global.asax.csLine 42

Explanation

Local OS environment access detected.

If you are targeting Managed Instance on Azure App Service, Read config via App Settings or App Configuration; avoid machine‑specific environment APIs. Persist environment setup via install scripts when needed.

When running in Azure App Service environment, your application can read environment variables that you define in App Service settings. Using environment API other than reading environment variables might indicate that your application depends on some local machine's features and might be broken on App Service sandbox or not scale well. Review your scenarios and either refactor them to be more cloud friendly or choose the option in App Service to host your application in the sandbox for Windows Container Web Apps.

If you choose to use other Azure hosting options such as Azure Container Apps (ACA) or Azure Kubernetes Service (AKS), environment APIs might work, however scaling still might be an issue.
Session state stored in-proc or in local process is detected
 Potential 3
FilePosition
src\eShopLegacyMVC\Web.config

Explanation

Session state stored in-proc or in local process is detected.

If you are targeting Managed Instance on Azure App Service, move session to Azure Cache for Redis or Cosmos DB. In-proc session impedes scale-out; Managed Instance does not change session semantics.

While if targeting other Azure compute services:

In-proc or local process stored session state not immediately prevents an application from working in Azure, however, is not recommended because it would make scaling the Azure App Service or Azure Kubernetes Service more difficult.

Azure provides multiple ways to store session state in a scalable way using Azure Cache for Redis, Azure Cosmos DB or other services.

Upgrade to newer target framework to get better cloud experience
 Optional 3
FilePosition
eShopLegacy.Utilities\eShopLegacy.Utilities.csproj
eShopPorted\eShopPorted.csproj

Explanation

Upgrade to newer target framework to get better cloud experience.

If you are targeting Managed Instance on Azure App Service, validate on .NET Framework 4.8 or move to .NET 10. Persist any runtime prerequisites via install scripts; test in staging before production.

While if targeting other Azure compute services:

Application targeting .NET framework lower than 4.7.1 might missing features that would be needed for some cloud scenarios like scaling or getting secrets from secure external sources.

Azure App Service runs apps on .NET Framework 4.8 or .NET Framework 3.5. Apps running on on .NET Framework versions older than .NET Framework 4.8 could have potential compatibility issues. It is recommended to test your application running on .NET Framework 4.8. Note that it is not necessary to re-target to .NET Framework 4.8, only to validate that the app correctly runs on that version of .NET Framework.

In the long term it is also recommended to upgrade your application to latest supported .NET 8+ which would significantly increase performance of your application. Use tools like .NET Upgrade Assistant to help with upgrading your application to newer .NET.

Deprecated Remoting & Serialization
 Mandatory 4
FilePosition

Explanation

Legacy .NET Remoting, BinaryFormatter, and related serialization APIs that are deprecated and removed for security reasons. Remoting provided distributed object communication but had significant security vulnerabilities. Migrate to gRPC, HTTP APIs, or modern serialization (System.Text.Json, protobuf).
Legacy Configuration System
 Mandatory 2
FilePosition

Explanation

Legacy XML-based configuration system (app.config/web.config) that has been replaced by a more flexible configuration model in .NET Core. The old system was rigid and XML-based. Migrate to Microsoft.Extensions.Configuration with JSON/environment variables; use System.Configuration.ConfigurationManager NuGet package as interim bridge if needed.
ASP.NET Framework (System.Web)
 Mandatory 4
FilePosition

Explanation

Legacy ASP.NET Framework APIs for web applications (System.Web.*) that don't exist in ASP.NET Core due to architectural differences. ASP.NET Core represents a complete redesign of the web framework. Migrate to ASP.NET Core equivalents or consider System.Web.Adapters package for compatibility.

Data Storage & External Services

The legacy project configures CatalogDBContext to use SQL Server LocalDB. The ASP.NET Core port configures a separate DefaultConnection to SQL Server LocalDB and uses Entity Framework Core. No external APIs, caches, or message brokers are configured for these applications; catalog images are served from the legacy application's local Pics directory.

Key Architectural Decisions

  • Both applications separate MVC controllers from catalog operations behind ICatalogService.
  • Autofac configures dependency injection in both applications, with mock-data implementations selectable from configuration.
  • The port is a distinct application using ASP.NET Core MVC and EF Core rather than a shared runtime with the legacy MVC app.

DTOs & Contracts

CatalogItem, CatalogBrand, and CatalogType are domain entities used by catalog services and views. PaginatedItemsViewModel is the paginated view response contract. Both applications define a BrandDTO nested in FilesController to shape the binary file response; these are mutable classes, not immutable records. The legacy MVC application's /api action returns an anonymous JSON message. No OpenAPI/Swagger document, protobuf schema, GraphQL schema, or gateway-level aggregation DTO was found. JSON responses use framework defaults; the files endpoints use a custom binary serializer.

Communication Patterns

All observed API and UI operations use synchronous HTTP request/response handling and direct in-process calls to ICatalogService; database operations are synchronous. No asynchronous messaging, service discovery, API gateway, client-side load balancing, retry policy, timeout policy, circuit breaker, or bulkhead configuration was found. The applications do not call one another or compose responses from downstream services. Startup initializes dependency injection and routing before handling requests.

No API-level authentication, authorization checks, or HTTPS/TLS enforcement were identified in the application code or route configuration. The APIs are therefore not protected by application-level identity or role checks in the inspected configuration.

Core Business Workflows

The application supports a product catalog: users browse, inspect, and maintain items categorized by brand and type. The legacy application and its port implement parallel catalog behavior without coordinating business data between them.

Domain Entities

EntityService / Bounded ContextDescriptionKey Relationships
CatalogItemeShopLegacyMVC / eShopPorted — CatalogProduct offered in the catalog, including pricing, stock, and image referenceBelongs to one brand and one type
CatalogBrandeShopLegacyMVC / eShopPorted — CatalogBrand used to classify catalog itemsCan classify multiple items
CatalogTypeeShopLegacyMVC / eShopPorted — CatalogProduct category or typeCan classify multiple items

Service-to-Domain Mapping

ServiceDomain ContextOwned EntitiesExternal Dependencies
eShopLegacyMVCCatalogCatalogItem, CatalogBrand, CatalogTypeIts configured SQL Server database or mock catalog service
eShopPortedCatalogCatalogItem, CatalogBrand, CatalogTypeIts configured SQL Server database or mock catalog service

Both applications implement their own catalog service and persistence context. No external business service or cross-context data exchange was identified.

Primary Workflows

Workflow 1: Browse the Catalog

  1. A user opens the catalog list or a specific item.
  2. The controller requests a paginated item list or item detail from the catalog service.
  3. The service loads the item and its brand/type classifications.
  4. The application renders the catalog view. Missing or invalid item identifiers produce a client error or not-found response.

Workflow 2: Maintain a Catalog Item

  1. A user opens the create or edit form; the application supplies available brand and type choices.
  2. On submission, the controller checks model validity and the anti-forgery token.
  3. If valid, the catalog service creates or updates the item and persists the change; otherwise the form is returned for correction.
  4. Successful create/update redirects to the catalog list. Deletion is confirmed before the item is removed.

The same core flows are implemented in both applications. The legacy implementation assigns new catalog item IDs using a SQL sequence; the ported implementation uses its configured EF Core key behavior.

Cross-Service Data Flows

No cross-service composition or aggregation occurs. The two applications maintain separate catalog stores and do not call or synchronize with each other. Within each application, catalog item reads include the associated brand and type; no downstream-service fallback behavior exists.

Business Workflow Sequence

sequenceDiagram participant User as "Catalog user" participant Controller as "Catalog controller" participant Service as "Catalog service" participant Store as "Catalog data store" User->>Controller: Submit catalog item changes Controller->>Controller: Validate form and anti-forgery token alt Input is valid Controller->>Service: Create or update item Service->>Store: Persist catalog change Store-->>Service: Change saved Service-->>Controller: Operation completed Controller-->>User: Redirect to catalog list else Input is invalid Controller-->>User: Return form with validation errors end

Business Rules & Decision Logic

  • Catalog item names are required. Price must be within the configured range and match the expected decimal format; stock, restock threshold, and maximum stock have configured numeric ranges.
  • Create and edit operations proceed only when model validation succeeds; form submissions include anti-forgery validation.
  • Item details and edit/delete views check that the item exists; missing IDs return a not-found response.
  • Deletion is initiated through a confirmation page. The brand API's demo delete action reports success for an existing brand but does not actually remove it.
  • Brand and type associations are required for catalog items in the ORM mappings. The catalog has no explicit lifecycle state machine, approval flow, or computed pricing rule.
  • Persistence uses ORM save operations; no explicit multi-operation transaction, audit trail, business authorization policy, retry, or compensating workflow was identified. Logging records application actions, but is not a separate business audit stream.

Version & Compatibility Risks

The port targets .NET Framework 4.6.1 while using ASP.NET Core 2.2 and EF Core 2.2, and the legacy application targets .NET Framework 4.7.2 with EF 6.2. These framework and package generations are old and require compatibility review for supported .NET targets. ASP.NET Core 2.2 and EF Core 2.2 are end-of-support; the solution also carries version skew in Newtonsoft.Json across projects.

Notable Observations

  • The solution contains two distinct web stacks and ORM generations, so modernization work should preserve each application's boundaries.
  • Autofac and log4net are shared across both applications, while the port references the legacy Autofac.Mvc5 package despite using ASP.NET Core MVC.
  • The legacy package inventory includes numerous system and UI support packages; the port separately declares old ASP.NET Core and EF Core packages.

No data/query caching provider or cache-aside pattern was identified. The applications provide mock catalog service implementations, but these are selected as alternate data sources rather than a cache; the port enables mock data in its default settings.

The legacy and ported applications each own a catalog schema in a separate configured database, with parallel Catalog, CatalogBrand, and CatalogType models. No cross-service API calls, shared database access, or synchronization mechanism between the applications was identified.
